title: the Sama Veda as song
hook: three singers sit down to talk shop, and one keeps asking: what holds that up? the answer goes all the way to space

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sama Veda as song, and the stobhas: small sounds between the words, which the Chandogya pairs with earth, wind and moon.

Why is the sky blue? Because of the light. Why? Because of the air. Why? Small children play this at bedtime, and the questions stop only when someone runs out of answers, or patience. The Chandogya Upanishad tells a story that runs like that. Three men skilled in the high chant of the Sama Veda sit down to talk about it, two brahmins and a king. And one question keeps getting asked, each time one step further down: what does that rest on?
screen: `WHY? BECAUSE. WHY?` → `THREE SINGERS SIT DOWN TOGETHER.` → `WHAT HOLDS UP A SONG?`

segments.voice: Their names are Shilaka, Dalbhya and Pravahana. Pravahana, the king, says: you two speak first; I'll listen. So Shilaka asks Dalbhya, in paraphrase: what does the saman, the chant, rest on? Dalbhya says: on tone, the sound of the voice. And tone? On breath. And breath? On food. And food? On water. And water? On that world, the heavens. And the heavens? Here Dalbhya stops. We don't lead the chant past the heavens, he says; we set it there. Shilaka isn't satisfied. The heavens, he says, rest on this world, the earth beneath us. Then Shilaka puts the question to the king: and this world, what does it rest on? Pravahana's answer: on space. All beings come out of space and go back into space, he says. Space is greater than all of them, the last support. And that, he says, is the high chant at its best: without end. Look at the shape of it. A song rests on a voice, the voice on breath, the breath on food, the food on water, and on down until the floor under everything is open room, not a thing but the space things happen in. A note only rings because there's air and room around it; sing into a pillow and it dies. It took three people, patience, and one more question to get there.
screen: `TWO BRAHMINS AND A KING.` · `TONE, BREATH, FOOD, WATER, HEAVEN.` · `AND THE EARTH? IT RESTS ON SPACE.` · `A NOTE RINGS BECAUSE THERE IS ROOM.`

segments.voice: At the end of each out-breath there's a small pause before the next breath comes; let your attention rest there without stretching it. Then listen for the quiet between one sound and the next, and the gap after a passing thought, the open room everything else happens in. If you pray, rest in prayer there.
The Sama Veda as song. In the Chandogya, three singers ask what the chant rests on: tone, breath, food, water, heaven, earth, and at last, space. Today's word.
screen: `THE SAMA VEDA AS SONG — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the Sama Veda as song. Underneath it all, there is open room. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1278 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE SAMA VEDA AS SONG.`

howItsDone: The dialogue of Shilaka, Dalbhya and King Pravahana is taught from the Chandogya Upanishad, part of the Sama Veda's tradition, as a meditation on the high chant resting finally on space.

fork.setup: you're Dalbhya. the chain has reached the heavens. Shilaka asks: and what do the heavens rest on?
options: stop: we set the chant in the heavens
fork.reveal: Dalbhya stops there and won't lead the chant past the heavens. the conversation goes on without him: Shilaka names the earth, and the king names space.

original.note: Sanskrit: space, open room. In Chandogya 1.9 it is the last support of the high chant.

trapdoor: what you thought: a song rests on a good voice.
what it means: in the Chandogya, the chant rests on tone, breath, food, water, heaven, earth, and finally space.
what a scholar hears: gati, 'support' or 'goal', asked again and again until Pravahana answers ākāśa, from which all beings arise and into which they return (Chandogya 1.8–1.9).
recall: stilling the movements of the mind

chat.says: In that Chandogya story, what does the king say the world rests on?
options: On space: all beings come out of it and go back into it, the last support.
On the heavens, and nothing past them, just as Dalbhya first said.
On water, since food and breath both come from it in the chain.
chat.meaning: In Chandogya 1.8–9, Dalbhya stops at the heavens and Shilaka at the earth; King Pravahana says space, greater than all beings, is the last support.

Pravahana.meaning: the king who listens first, then answers: space

Shilaka.meaning: a singer who presses the question past the heavens

Dalbhya.meaning: a singer who stops the chain at the heavens

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 1.8 (Shilaka, Dalbhya and Pravahana: the chant rests on tone, breath, food, water, the heavens, the earth)
Chandogya Upanishad 1.9.1–2 (all beings arise from space and return to it; space is the final support; the udgitha is without end)

notes: Names given in short form: Śilaka Śālāvatya, Caikitāyana Dālbhya, Pravāhaṇa Jaivali; confirm 'two priests and a king' (Pravāhaṇa as a kṣatriya king; the other two as brahmins).

Order of the chain (svara, prāṇa, anna, āpaḥ, 'that world', 'this world', ākāśa) and who says which step are given from memory; confirm. In the text Dālbhya stops at 'that world' and Śilaka names 'this world'.
'Without end' for the udgitha as parovarīyas / ananta in 1.9.2; confirm the paraphrase.
'Sing into a pillow and it dies' is an everyday illustration, not a claim about the text.

Editor pass: 'two priests' changed to 'two brahmins' (Pravahana's own word in 1.8); the final question is now put to the king by Shilaka, as in the text, rather than asked by the king himself; the practice was rewritten (rest in the pauses between breaths, sounds and thoughts) because the floor-ground-space body scan repeated 1262, 1265 and 1275.
